issues.explanation: Gunshot noise is difficult to reconcile as a primary trauma-linked trigger for childhood physical abuse by a caregiver, especially when no other items suggest weapon-related or combat/shooting associations.

issues.item: Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin
issues.explanation: A highly specific temperature-on-skin trigger is not impossible, but with the rest of the profile it lacks a plausible link to the stated trauma and is unsupported by memory or threat content; together with gunshot noise it makes the trigger set feel clinically disconnected from caregiver physical abuse.

issues.item: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body
issues.explanation: For childhood physical abuse by a caregiver, the profile is otherwise organized around shame/self-concept and social avoidance. 'Body Unreliable' is less coherent with the rest of the selected items because there are no accompanying threat or memory items indicating prominent somatic threat, dissociation, injury-related beliefs, or body-based trauma processing. Within this formulation, Negative Appraisals is strongly linked to maladaptive avoidance and modestly linked with triggers; the other appraisals fit that pattern, but this item introduces a distinct body-failure theme that is not supported elsewhere in the profile.

vignette:
Rohan Mehta is a 36-year-old South Asian American detective, married, who presented for treatment following what he described as a gradual but accelerating collapse of his ability to function at work and at home. His PCL-5 score of 74 reflects a severe symptom burden that has been building, he acknowledged quietly in the first session, for most of his life - though it was only in recent months that he could no longer contain it.

Rohan grew up in a household where his father's rages were unpredictable and physical. The abuse was not occasional; it was woven into the texture of childhood. What Rohan remembers most viscerally is not any single incident but a constellation of sensations that announced what was coming: the particular cold of a winter morning when his father would drag him from bed, the sharp crack of a door thrown open against the wall before the footsteps reached him, the chill of the air against his skin in those suspended seconds before contact. His father favored the early hours, when the house was dark and everyone else was asleep, and so Rohan learned very young that being alone in a room at night meant being unprotected, and that the sound of a door was not a neutral thing.

He left home at eighteen and built, by most external measures, a formidable life. He became a detective, drawn perhaps to the idea of being the person who arrives after the violence rather than the one waiting for it. For years the work absorbed him. But in the past year, something shifted. The precinct is a loud, physical environment - doors slam constantly as officers move through the building, and on cold mornings the temperature in the older interview rooms drops sharply before the heating catches. Rohan found himself freezing at his desk when the thermostat dipped, a specific coolness against his forearms that stopped him mid-sentence, mid-thought. He began wearing long sleeves year-round and positioning himself near the radiator, habits his colleagues noticed but did not understand. When a door slammed down the corridor during an interview, he would feel his body respond before his mind could intervene - a full-body alertness that he was certain any experienced detective could read on his face.

At home, the symptoms pressed differently. Rohan began staying up until two or three in the morning, finding reasons to remain downstairs while his wife slept. He told her he was reviewing case files. What he could not tell her was that lying alone in a dark room, in the particular quiet of the early hours, felt unbearable in a way he had no language for. On nights when she traveled for work, he did not sleep at all. He had come to believe that something about being alone in the dark made him genuinely unsafe, though he could not articulate to himself what the threat was or where it would come from.

Over the past several months, Rohan began declining social invitations, first the ones that required effort and then the ones that did not. He stopped going to the gym, then to the grocery store on weekends, preferring to send his wife. His world contracted. His sergeant commented that he seemed distracted and recommended he speak to the department's occupational health service, which he did not do. His wife, patient and perceptive, eventually told him she was frightened - not of him, but for him.

What troubles Rohan most, sitting in the intake chair, is not the triggers or the sleeplessness but the conclusions he has drawn about himself from all of it. He is certain that a man in his profession, who has interviewed trauma survivors and testified in court and worked homicide scenes, should not be undone by a cold room or a slamming door. He feels like a lousy coper, he said, using that exact phrase, and when pressed he went further: he no longer recognizes himself, and he suspects, with a quiet and terrible certainty, that whatever is wrong with him is not circumstantial but constitutional - something broken at the core. It was his wife's fear, more than his own, that finally brought him in. What he is most hoping for, he said, is to understand why he is this way. What he is most afraid of is that there will be a clear answer.
